items.prompt: Checkout calls the email service directly and waits for a response. What specific problem does putting a queue between them fix?
choices: It makes the email service faster
It removes checkout's dependency on the email service's speed and availability — checkout only waits for the queue to accept the message
It guarantees the email is grammatically correct
It makes the email service optional
items.explanation: A queue decouples timing: the producer's response time no longer depends on how fast (or whether) the consumer processes the message, only on the queue accepting it. The consumer can be slow, restarting, or briefly down without that becoming the producer's problem.
items.reference:
Checkout → direct call → Email

Why: a direct call ties the caller's response time and retry behavior to the callee's health; a queue in between removes that coupling.

items.prompt: In the L1 Scenario, why did a slow email service cause checkout itself to become slow?
choices: Checkout and email shared the same database
Checkout called email synchronously over HTTP and waited for the response before continuing
The email service was written in a slower language
Checkout always waits 30 seconds between requests
items.explanation: A synchronous, direct call makes the caller's latency include the callee's latency. Checkout couldn't tell the customer 'order placed' until the email call returned, so a slow email service directly became a slow checkout.
items.reference:
Checkout → direct call → Email

Why: a direct call ties the caller's response time and retry behavior to the callee's health; a queue in between removes that coupling.

items.prompt: With a queue in place, what does the checkout service actually wait for before responding to the customer?
choices: Nothing at all — it never waits
The email being fully delivered to the customer's inbox
The queue confirming it accepted the enqueued message
The email worker restarting if it had crashed
items.explanation: Checkout's remaining dependency is only on the queue accepting the write — a much smaller, more reliable promise than 'the email service processed this successfully,' which is exactly what got decoupled.
items.reference:
Checkout → direct call → Email

Why: a direct call ties the caller's response time and retry behavior to the callee's health; a queue in between removes that coupling.

items.prompt: Which delivery guarantee never loses a message but may deliver it more than once?
choices: At-most-once
At-least-once
Exactly-once
None of these ever lose or duplicate messages
items.explanation: At-least-once guarantees a message is delivered one or more times — it trades the possibility of a duplicate for the certainty of never silently dropping a message.
items.reference:
GuaranteeCan lose?Can duplicate?
At-most-onceYesNo
At-least-onceNoYes
Exactly-onceNoNo

Why: each guarantee accepts a different failure mode; most production queues pick at-least-once because losing a message is worse than seeing it twice.

items.prompt: Which delivery guarantee can silently drop a message, but never delivers it twice?
choices: At-most-once
At-least-once
Exactly-once
FIFO
items.explanation: At-most-once delivers a message zero or one times — it never retries on failure, so a message can vanish without a trace, but a delivered message is never duplicated.
items.reference:
GuaranteeCan lose?Can duplicate?
At-most-onceYesNo
At-least-onceNoYes
Exactly-onceNoNo

Why: each guarantee accepts a different failure mode; most production queues pick at-least-once because losing a message is worse than seeing it twice.

items.prompt: Why do most production queues (SQS, RabbitMQ, default-mode Kafka) default to at-least-once rather than at-most-once?
choices: At-least-once is easier to implement
Losing a message silently is almost always worse than seeing it twice, provided the consumer can handle duplicates safely
At-most-once was deprecated by industry standards
At-least-once is always faster
items.explanation: At-most-once risks silent data loss with no retry; at-least-once risks a duplicate, which is a solvable problem on the consumer side (idempotency). Given the choice, most systems would rather handle a duplicate than lose data outright.
items.reference:
GuaranteeCan lose?Can duplicate?
At-most-onceYesNo
At-least-onceNoYes
Exactly-onceNoNo

Why: each guarantee accepts a different failure mode; most production queues pick at-least-once because losing a message is worse than seeing it twice.

items.prompt: A system advertises 'exactly-once processing.' What is it most likely actually doing under the hood?
choices: Guaranteeing the network never fails
Combining at-least-once delivery from the queue with idempotent processing on the consumer, so a duplicate delivery has no extra effect
Using a faster network protocol
Storing every message twice for safety
items.explanation: True end-to-end exactly-once delivery is extremely hard to guarantee. What's actually happening in almost every real system is at-least-once delivery paired with an idempotent consumer — the queue's promise (never lose) plus the consumer's promise (never double the effect) add up to an exactly-once outcome.
items.reference:
Queue's job: never lose a message (at-least-once)
Consumer's job: processing the same message twice has the same effect as once (idempotent)

Why: 'exactly-once' in practice is usually this division of labor, not one single mechanism.

items.prompt: If a queue delivers the same 'send confirmation email' message twice, but the customer still only receives one email, what made that true?
choices: The queue silently discarded the duplicate on its own
The consumer recognized it had already processed that message and skipped sending a second email
Email providers automatically deduplicate
It was luck — this isn't something you can design for
items.explanation: This is idempotent processing in action: the consumer detects it already handled this exact message and skips the side effect on the repeat, even though the queue genuinely delivered it twice.
items.reference:
Queue's job: never lose a message (at-least-once)
Consumer's job: processing the same message twice has the same effect as once (idempotent)

Why: 'exactly-once' in practice is usually this division of labor, not one single mechanism.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between 'at-least-once delivery' and 'idempotent processing'?
choices: They're competing alternatives — a system picks one or the other
Idempotent processing is what makes at-least-once delivery safe to build on, by making a duplicate delivery harmless
Idempotent processing replaces the need for a queue entirely
At-least-once delivery already implies idempotent processing automatically
items.explanation: They're complementary, not competing: at-least-once delivery is the easier guarantee for a queue to keep, and idempotent processing is what neutralizes the duplicates that guarantee allows, together producing an exactly-once effect.
items.reference:
Queue's job: never lose a message (at-least-once)
Consumer's job: processing the same message twice has the same effect as once (idempotent)

Why: 'exactly-once' in practice is usually this division of labor, not one single mechanism.

items.prompt: In the queue diagram (producer enqueues, consumer delivers when ready, consumer acks), what does the consumer send back to the queue once it's done?
choices: A new message
An acknowledgment that it processed the message
The original request
Nothing — the queue polls the consumer instead
items.explanation: The consumer acknowledges (acks) back to the queue once it has finished processing, which tells the queue it's safe to remove the message permanently.
items.reference:
Producer
→
Queue
→
Consumer

Why: the producer only waits on the middle box, not the consumer's own processing time.

items.prompt: If the email worker crashes mid-shift while messages are waiting in the queue, what happens to those messages?
choices: They are lost permanently
They wait in the queue until a worker becomes available to read them
The producer is notified to resend everything from scratch
They are automatically converted to a different message type
items.explanation: This is the whole point of decoupling: messages simply sit in the queue, unaffected by the consumer's availability, until some worker — the same one restarted, or a different one — comes back and reads them.
items.reference:
Producer
→
Queue
→
Consumer

Why: the producer only waits on the middle box, not the consumer's own processing time.

items.prompt: A worker reads a message but crashes before sending any ack or nack. What does the queue do once the visibility timeout expires?
choices: Deletes the message permanently, assuming it was handled
Redelivers the message to another available consumer
Pauses the entire queue until manually resumed
Sends the message back to the original producer
items.explanation: With no ack or nack received before the visibility timeout expires, the queue assumes the worst — that the message was never actually handled — and redelivers it to another consumer, true to at-least-once delivery.
items.reference:
Ack: 'I'm done' → message deleted
Nack: 'I failed' → message visible again immediately
Timeout expires, no signal: queue assumes the worker died → redelivers

Why: the queue can't ask a dead worker what happened, so it uses a timer as its only signal.

items.prompt: What's the practical difference between a worker explicitly nacking a message versus doing nothing and letting the visibility timeout expire?
choices: There is no difference — both behave identically
Nacking triggers immediate redelivery; waiting for the timeout delays redelivery until the full timeout window passes
Nacking deletes the message; timing out redelivers it
Nacking only works on FIFO queues
items.explanation: Nacking is an active signal that gets a known-failed message back into circulation right away, instead of leaving it invisible (and unavailable to any other consumer) for the entire visibility timeout window for no reason.
items.reference:
Ack: 'I'm done' → message deleted
Nack: 'I failed' → message visible again immediately
Timeout expires, no signal: queue assumes the worker died → redelivers

Why: the queue can't ask a dead worker what happened, so it uses a timer as its only signal.

items.prompt: Why can't the queue simply ask a crashed worker whether it finished processing a message before deciding to redelivery it?
choices: The queue is not allowed to communicate with workers
A crashed process cannot respond to anything — the queue only has a timer to infer that something went wrong
Workers never crash in production
The queue always keeps a backup copy of every worker's state
items.explanation: A dead worker can't answer, so the visibility timeout is a proxy signal, not a direct one — the queue infers 'probably not handled' from silence, which is why it can't distinguish a worker that died before doing anything from one that died right after finishing but before acking.
items.reference:
Ack: 'I'm done' → message deleted
Nack: 'I failed' → message visible again immediately
Timeout expires, no signal: queue assumes the worker died → redelivers

Why: the queue can't ask a dead worker what happened, so it uses a timer as its only signal.

items.prompt: What is an idempotency key used for in a queue consumer?
choices: Encrypting the message payload
Recognizing that a message has already been fully processed, so a duplicate delivery can skip the side effect
Determining which consumer replica should get the message
Compressing the message before storage
items.explanation: An idempotency key — the message's own ID, or a stable business key — is checked against a store of already-processed keys before running a side effect, so a redelivered message is recognized and its effect is skipped, not repeated.
items.reference:
seen(key)? → skip side effect, ack
not seen? → run side effect, record key, ack

Why: the dedupe store must outlive the queue's max redelivery window, or it protects against nothing.

items.prompt: A team stores their idempotency keys in an in-memory JS Set that resets whenever the worker process restarts. What's wrong with this?
choices: Nothing — Sets are always the right choice
The exact scenario that triggers redelivery (a worker restarting) is also the scenario that wipes the dedupe store, so it protects against nothing
Sets can't store strings
It's too slow for production use
items.explanation: A worker crashing and restarting is precisely the situation that causes redelivery in the first place. If the dedupe store lives only in that worker's memory, it's gone exactly when it's needed most — the store has to be shared and durable across restarts and replicas.
items.reference:
seen(key)? → skip side effect, ack
not seen? → run side effect, record key, ack

Why: the dedupe store must outlive the queue's max redelivery window, or it protects against nothing.

items.prompt: Why does the dedupe store's time-to-live (TTL) need to exceed the queue's maximum possible redelivery window?
choices: It doesn't matter what the TTL is set to
If the key expires before redelivery could still plausibly happen, a genuinely-duplicate message will look brand new and get processed again
A longer TTL makes the queue itself faster
TTL only affects how the message is displayed in dashboards
items.explanation: If the dedupe key is forgotten before the queue's redelivery window has passed, a duplicate delivery arriving after that point finds no record of having been seen before — the protection silently lapses exactly when a late redelivery still could arrive.
items.reference:
seen(key)? → skip side effect, ack
not seen? → run side effect, record key, ack

Why: the dedupe store must outlive the queue's max redelivery window, or it protects against nothing.

items.prompt: Does a standard (non-FIFO) queue guarantee messages come out in the same order they were written?
choices: Yes, always, regardless of queue type
No — concurrent consumers naturally interleave, so order isn't guaranteed unless a FIFO/partitioned queue is used
Only if there's exactly one producer
Only for messages under 1KB
items.explanation: A standard queue makes no ordering promise — multiple consumers pulling concurrently will naturally process messages out of order. A FIFO or partitioned queue is needed to preserve order, and even then usually only within a given ordering key.
items.reference:
TypeOrder guarantee
Standard queueNone
FIFO / partitionedWithin one ordering key only

Why: guaranteeing global order across every producer rarely scales, so ordering is usually scoped to a key.

items.prompt: A FIFO queue guarantees order 'within a given ordering key' (e.g. all messages for one orderId). Why not just guarantee global order across every message from every producer?
choices: It's technically impossible in any system
Global ordering across every producer rarely scales — scoping order to a key trades a weaker guarantee for much better throughput
Global ordering was never useful for anything
FIFO queues don't support multiple producers
items.explanation: Enforcing a single global order forces effectively single-threaded processing across the entire queue. Scoping the guarantee to an ordering key (like orderId) lets unrelated keys process fully in parallel, which is the throughput trade-off almost every real system needs.
items.reference:
TypeOrder guarantee
Standard queueNone
FIFO / partitionedWithin one ordering key only

Why: guaranteeing global order across every producer rarely scales, so ordering is usually scoped to a key.

items.prompt: What is a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for?
choices: Storing messages that were successfully processed, as a backup
Holding messages that failed processing repeatedly, after a configured retry limit, so they stop looping and wait for review
Speeding up delivery for high-priority messages
Permanently deleting messages the system doesn't recognize
items.explanation: A DLQ is where a message goes after it has failed processing a configured number of times — rather than retrying forever and burning worker capacity on something that can't succeed, it's routed aside for a human or repair job to look at.
items.reference:
Attempt 1 fail→Attempt 2 fail→Attempt 3 fail: max hit→DLQ

Why: a message that can never succeed shouldn't retry forever, burning worker time on the impossible.

items.prompt: A team sets their DLQ's max-retry count to 1. What risk does this introduce compared to a higher count like 5?
choices: None — lower retry counts are always safer
A transient failure (a brief timeout, a service mid-deploy) that would likely succeed on a second try instead gets exiled to the DLQ immediately
It makes messages process faster on the first attempt
It only affects FIFO queues, not standard ones
items.explanation: A retry count of 1 stops distinguishing transient failures (which usually resolve on their own within a few attempts) from permanent ones — every single hiccup, however brief, gets treated the same as an unfixable message and pushed to the DLQ.
items.reference:
Attempt 1 fail→Attempt 2 fail→Attempt 3 fail: max hit→DLQ

Why: a message that can never succeed shouldn't retry forever, burning worker time on the impossible.

items.prompt: Without a DLQ, what happens to a message with a permanently malformed payload that a consumer can never successfully parse?
choices: It gets automatically fixed by the queue
It retries and fails forever, endlessly consuming worker time without ever succeeding
It's silently dropped after the first failure
The consumer stops processing all other messages until it's fixed
items.explanation: Without a DLQ (or a max-retry cutoff), a message that can never succeed just keeps getting redelivered and keeps failing — an infinite loop that consumes worker capacity that could otherwise go to messages that actually can succeed.
items.reference:
Attempt 1 fail→Attempt 2 fail→Attempt 3 fail: max hit→DLQ

Why: a message that can never succeed shouldn't retry forever, burning worker time on the impossible.

items.prompt: If producers write messages faster than consumers can process them for a sustained period, what happens?
choices: The queue automatically speeds up the consumers
Queue depth grows without bound, and the queue alone doesn't fix this — it only buys time
The producer is automatically blocked from writing more
Messages are automatically deleted to make room
items.explanation: A queue is a buffer, not a rate-matching mechanism — if the write rate consistently exceeds the processing rate, depth simply grows. Real systems need monitoring on queue depth/consumer lag plus a plan (scale consumers, shed load) to actually resolve the mismatch.
items.reference:
Producer rate > consumer rate
→
queue depth grows unbounded

Why: a queue buys time under load, it doesn't fix the underlying rate mismatch on its own.

items.prompt: Why is monitoring consumer lag (or queue depth) considered a necessary companion to using a queue, not an optional nicety?
choices: It's only useful for billing purposes
A queue can silently absorb a growing backlog for a long time before anyone notices, until the buffer itself becomes the outage
Queues automatically alert engineers without any monitoring setup
It has no real operational value
items.explanation: Because a queue's whole job is to absorb a temporary mismatch, a real, sustained mismatch can hide behind a growing-but-not-yet-alarming backlog for a while — without monitoring, that backlog keeps growing until it becomes a full-blown outage instead of an early warning.
items.reference:
Producer rate > consumer rate
→
queue depth grows unbounded

Why: a queue buys time under load, it doesn't fix the underlying rate mismatch on its own.

items.prompt: Implement markIfNew(seen, key) where seen is a Set<string>. It should return true and add the key the first time a key is seen, and return false (without changing the set) on every call after that for the same key.

tests.description: first call with a new key returns true
second call with the same key returns false
tests.expr: const s = new Set(); markIfNew(s, 'msg-1'); expect(markIfNew(s, 'msg-1')).toBe(false)

tests.description: a different key is independent
tests.expr: const s = new Set(); markIfNew(s, 'msg-1'); expect(markIfNew(s, 'msg-2')).toBe(true)

items.explanation: Checking seen.has(key) first and only calling seen.add(key) when it's genuinely new keeps 'already seen' keys from being processed a second time. In a single-threaded, in-process context like this exercise, has-then-add is enough — but in a real distributed consumer (L3's DedupeStore), that same two-step check must happen as one atomic operation, or two workers racing on the same key can both see 'not seen yet' before either finishes recording it.
items.reference:
markIfNew(store, key)
→ true (first time)
→ false (already seen)

Why: the check-and-record has to be a single atomic step, or two concurrent callers can both pass the check before either records the result.

items.prompt: Implement countNewMessages(seen, keys) where seen is a Set<string> and keys is an array of message IDs (possibly with repeats). Return how many of the keys in the array are new (not already in seen, and not repeated earlier in the same array).

tests.description: all-new keys are all counted
a key already in seen is not counted
a repeat within the same array is only counted once

items.explanation: Each key has to be checked against the running state of `seen` as it goes, not against the original set alone — that's what makes an in-array repeat only count once, the same way a redelivered message shouldn't be processed twice even within one batch.
items.reference:
markIfNew(store, key)
→ true (first time)
→ false (already seen)

Why: the check-and-record has to be a single atomic step, or two concurrent callers can both pass the check before either records the result.

items.prompt: Implement processIfNew(seen, key, sideEffect) where seen is a Set<string> and sideEffect is a zero-argument function. Call sideEffect() and return its result only if key is new; if key was already seen, don't call sideEffect and return undefined.

tests.description: new key runs the side effect and returns its result
already-seen key does not run the side effect
tests.expr: const s = new Set(['k']); let called = false; processIfNew(s, 'k', () => { called = true; return 1; }); expect(called).toBe(false)

tests.description: already-seen key returns undefined

items.explanation: This is the shape of L3's processChargeMessage in miniature: the side effect (charging a card, in the real version) only runs when the idempotency key hasn't been seen before, and a duplicate delivery becomes a harmless no-op instead of a repeated charge.
items.reference:
markIfNew(store, key)
→ true (first time)
→ false (already seen)

Why: the check-and-record has to be a single atomic step, or two concurrent callers can both pass the check before either records the result.

items.prompt: Implement backoffCeiling(attempt, baseDelayMs, maxDelayMs) (attempt is 1-indexed) returning baseDelayMs * 2^(attempt-1), capped at maxDelayMs. No randomness — this computes the ceiling jitter would be applied under.

tests.description: attempt 1 returns the base delay
attempt 3 doubles twice
a large attempt is capped at maxDelayMs

items.explanation: Each attempt's ceiling doubles the previous one (2^(attempt-1) growth), which is what makes retries spread out over time instead of hammering a struggling system at a fixed interval. The Math.min cap stops the delay from growing unboundedly on a long string of failures.
items.reference:
attempt 1: base
attempt 2: base × 2
attempt 3: base × 4
...capped at maxDelayMs

Why: the delay grows with each attempt so retries back off instead of hammering an already-struggling system, and the cap keeps it from growing forever.

items.prompt: Implement attemptsUntilCapped(baseDelayMs, maxDelayMs) returning the smallest attempt number (1-indexed) at which baseDelayMs * 2^(attempt-1) first reaches or exceeds maxDelayMs.

tests.description: base 200, max 200 is capped on attempt 1
base 200, max 800 is capped on attempt 3
base 200, max 6400 is capped on attempt 6

items.explanation: This walks the same doubling sequence as backoffCeiling until it first reaches the cap — useful for reasoning about how many attempts actually see meaningfully different delays before the cap flattens the curve, which is exactly what the L3 xychart-beta chart shows visually.
items.reference:
attempt 1: base
attempt 2: base × 2
attempt 3: base × 4
...capped at maxDelayMs

Why: the delay grows with each attempt so retries back off instead of hammering an already-struggling system, and the cap keeps it from growing forever.

items.prompt: Implement withinJitterRange(delay, ceiling) returning true if delay is a valid 'full jitter' value for that ceiling — that is, 0 <= delay <= ceiling — and false otherwise.

tests.description: a delay of 0 is valid
a delay equal to the ceiling is valid
a delay above the ceiling is invalid
a negative delay is invalid

items.explanation: 'Full jitter' picks a random delay anywhere between 0 and the computed ceiling, rather than always waiting the full ceiling — this spreads concurrent retries out across that whole range so they don't all wake up on the same tick, which is what actually prevents the thundering-herd effect.
items.reference:
attempt 1: base
attempt 2: base × 2
attempt 3: base × 4
...capped at maxDelayMs

Why: the delay grows with each attempt so retries back off instead of hammering an already-struggling system, and the cap keeps it from growing forever.

items.prompt: Implement decideRouting(attemptNumber, maxAttempts, isPermanent) returning the string 'dead-letter' if isPermanent is true, or if attemptNumber >= maxAttempts; otherwise return 'retry'.

tests.description: a permanent error dead-letters on the first attempt
a transient error with attempts left retries
a transient error at the max attempt dead-letters

items.explanation: A permanent error skips straight to dead-letter regardless of attempt count, since retrying it can never succeed. A transient error gets to retry until attempts run out, at which point it also dead-letters — same destination, different reason for getting there.
items.reference:
Permanent error → dead-letter immediately
Transient error, attempts left → retry
Transient error, attempts exhausted → dead-letter

Why: a fact about the message (unfixable) and a fact about the moment (temporary outage) need different responses.

items.prompt: Implement attemptsWasted(maxAttempts, isPermanent) returning how many retry attempts were wasted on a message that was mis-categorized as transient (isPermanent === false) when it was actually permanent — i.e. how many attempts run before it finally dead-letters at maxAttempts. Return 0 if isPermanent is true (correctly categorized, no waste).

tests.description: correctly categorized as permanent wastes nothing
mis-categorized as transient wastes maxAttempts - 1 tries
a maxAttempts of 1 wastes nothing even if mis-categorized

items.explanation: A genuinely permanent error thrown correctly dead-letters on attempt 1, wasting nothing. The same error mis-thrown as a plain (retryable) error burns through every attempt up to maxAttempts before finally dead-lettering — exactly the cost the L3 checkpoint on mis-categorization describes.
items.reference:
Permanent error → dead-letter immediately
Transient error, attempts left → retry
Transient error, attempts exhausted → dead-letter

Why: a fact about the message (unfixable) and a fact about the moment (temporary outage) need different responses.

items.prompt: Implement routingReason(attemptNumber, maxAttempts, isPermanent, errorMessage) returning a string: if isPermanent, return `permanent: ${errorMessage}`; else if attemptNumber >= maxAttempts, return `exceeded ${maxAttempts} attempts: ${errorMessage}`; otherwise return null.

tests.description: permanent error produces a permanent: reason
exhausted attempts produces an exceeded reason
a retryable case with attempts left returns null

items.explanation: Attaching a reason string to a dead-letter routing decision (rather than just a bare 'dead-letter' verdict) is what makes the DLQ actually useful to a human later — they can tell at a glance whether a message needs a code fix (permanent) or was just unlucky timing (exceeded attempts) without re-deriving it from scratch.
items.reference:
Permanent error → dead-letter immediately
Transient error, attempts left → retry
Transient error, attempts exhausted → dead-letter

Why: a fact about the message (unfixable) and a fact about the moment (temporary outage) need different responses.

items.prompt: Implement processCharge(store, messageId, chargeFn) where store is a Set<string>. If messageId is new, add it to store, call chargeFn() and return { charged: true, result: chargeFn's return value }. If messageId was already in store, don't call chargeFn and return { charged: false }.

tests.description: a new message id runs chargeFn and reports charged: true
the result of chargeFn is passed through
a duplicate message id does not run chargeFn again
tests.expr: const s = new Set(); processCharge(s, 'm1', () => 'ok'); let called = false; processCharge(s, 'm1', () => { called = true; }); expect(called).toBe(false)

items.explanation: Recording the message ID before returning ensures a second call with the same ID sees it already marked and skips the charge — this is the same shape as L3's processChargeMessage, just against a synchronous Set instead of an async distributed store.
items.reference:
processCharge(store, id, chargeFn)
→ {charged: true, ...} (first time)
→ {charged: false} (duplicate)

Why: the consumer still acks a skipped duplicate normally — skipping the side effect is not the same as failing the message.

items.prompt: Implement chargeCountFor(store, messageIds, chargeFn) where messageIds is an array of message IDs (possibly with duplicates) delivered in order. Call chargeFn() once per genuinely-new ID and return the total number of times chargeFn was actually called.

tests.description: three distinct ids call chargeFn three times
a redelivered id is only charged once
all ids already in store results in zero calls

items.explanation: This models a batch of redeliveries the way a real worker would see them over time: the store's state carries forward across the whole array, so a message repeated later in the batch is recognized as a duplicate exactly like a redelivery arriving minutes later would be.
items.reference:
processCharge(store, id, chargeFn)
→ {charged: true, ...} (first time)
→ {charged: false} (duplicate)

Why: the consumer still acks a skipped duplicate normally — skipping the side effect is not the same as failing the message.

items.prompt: Implement isDuplicateDelivery(store, messageId) — a read-only check, distinct from processCharge, that returns true if messageId is already in store without modifying store at all.

tests.description: an unseen id is not a duplicate
a seen id is a duplicate
calling it does not add the id to the store
tests.expr: const s = new Set(); isDuplicateDelivery(s, 'm1'); expect(s.has('m1')).toBe(false)

items.explanation: Keeping a pure read-only check separate from the check-and-record operation matters for reasoning about atomicity: a caller that wants to log or branch on 'is this a duplicate?' without side effects needs this, distinct from processCharge's check-and-set, which intentionally does both in one step.
items.reference:
processCharge(store, id, chargeFn)
→ {charged: true, ...} (first time)
→ {charged: false} (duplicate)

Why: the consumer still acks a skipped duplicate normally — skipping the side effect is not the same as failing the message.

items.prompt: Implement isExpired(recordedAt, ttlMs, now) returning true if now >= recordedAt + ttlMs (the dedupe key has expired), false otherwise. All arguments are millisecond timestamps/durations.

tests.description: before expiry is not expired
exactly at expiry counts as expired
well past expiry is expired

items.explanation: This is the arithmetic underneath L3's DEDUPE_TTL_MS discussion: a dedupe key is only useful while now is still before its expiry. Once now crosses that line, the key is gone and a redelivery arriving after that point is treated as brand new.
items.reference:
expiresAt = recordedAt + ttlMs
expired = now >= expiresAt

Why: once a dedupe key expires, a genuinely-late redelivery looks brand new and slips through.

items.prompt: Implement isDedupeWindowSafe(ttlMs, maxRedeliveryWindowMs) returning true if the dedupe TTL comfortably covers the queue's max possible redelivery window (ttlMs >= maxRedeliveryWindowMs), false otherwise.

tests.description: a TTL shorter than the redelivery window is unsafe
a TTL equal to the redelivery window is safe
a TTL longer than the redelivery window is safe

items.explanation: This is exactly the L3 checkpoint's scenario turned into a check: a 60-second TTL against a 5-minute (300,000ms) visibility timeout is unsafe, because a late redelivery arriving after the key expired would look brand new and get double-processed.
items.reference:
expiresAt = recordedAt + ttlMs
expired = now >= expiresAt

Why: once a dedupe key expires, a genuinely-late redelivery looks brand new and slips through.

items.prompt: In the L1 Scenario, the order got created twice because checkout's call to the email service timed out. What did checkout's retry logic actually resend?
choices: Just a ping to check if email was alive
The entire order creation request, not just the email step
A cancellation for the original order
Nothing — checkout does not retry automatically
items.explanation: Because checkout and email were coupled into one synchronous call, a timeout on that call triggered checkout's retry of the whole originating request — including the order creation — not just the email send, producing a duplicate order rather than just a duplicate email attempt.
items.reference:
Timeout, no response: caller retries the whole request → duplicate order
Response lost, work succeeded: caller retries → duplicate email

Why: both bugs come from the same root cause — a direct, synchronous call with no space between 'I sent this' and 'you received this.'

items.prompt: In the second failure described in the L1 Scenario, the email actually sent successfully. Why did the customer still get three copies?
choices: The email service has a bug that always sends multiple copies
The success response was lost on the way back to the caller, so the caller — seeing no response — retried the request
The customer manually requested extra copies
Email providers batch and resend automatically
items.explanation: The work itself succeeded, but the acknowledgment of that success never reached the caller. With no way to tell 'it worked but I didn't hear back' apart from 'it failed,' the caller retried — and each retry sent another real email, since the underlying send itself has no memory of the earlier attempt.

Response lost, work succeeded: caller retries → duplicate email

Why: both bugs come from the same root cause — a direct, synchronous call with no space between 'I sent this' and 'you received this.'
